title: Year 10 Mathematics (Standard)
exam_focus: Follows the 10MATP 26 Scope & Sequence and the format of the 2025 school half-yearly paper: interest and depreciation, income tax (tax tables, taxable income, PAYG and net income), algebra and index laws, equations and inequalities (including simultaneous equations), coordinate geometry and graphs of functions, right-angled trigonometry, surface area and volume, statistics (including standard deviation) and probability — nine strands.

questions.stem: Tomas earns $28 per hour for the first 38 hours he works each week. Any hours beyond 38 are paid at time-and-a-half. Last week he worked 45 hours. What was his total pay for the week?
questions.explanation_en: For the first 38 hours, 38×$28=$1,064, and for the 7 overtime hours (45−38=7), the pay is $42 per hour, so 7×$42=$294, for a total of $1,358; common mistakes include calculating the total as $1,260 using only the basic hourly rate for 45 hours, or $1,456 using double the hourly rate for overtime.
questions.source: Topic1 Interest and Depreciation.pdf · 1-01 Earning an income

questions.stem: Sophie deposits $1,200 into a savings account that earns 5% per annum, compounded monthly. How much will she have in the account after 3 years?
questions.explanation_en: For monthly compounding, convert both the interest rate and the number of periods to months: R=0.05/12, n=3×12=36, A=1200(1+0.05/12)^36≈$1,393.77; using simple interest gives $1,380, and using 5% as the annual interest rate with only 3 compounding periods gives $1,389.15, both of which are common mistakes.
questions.source: 1-04_ Compound Interest.pdf · A = P(1 + R)^n (R is the rate per period)

questions.stem: A delivery van is bought for $42,000. It depreciates at 15% per annum using the reducing-balance formula A = P(1 − R)^n. Find (a) its value after 4 years, correct to the nearest dollar, and (b) the total amount it has depreciated over those 4 years.
questions.explanation_en: The reducing balance depreciation is multiplied by 0.85 each year for 4 years, not 42,000×(1−0.15×4); using the straight-line method (reducing by a fixed $6,300 each year) gives $16,800, which is another model.
questions.source: 1-07_ Depreciation.pdf · A = P(1 − R)^n(reducing balance)

criteria.t: Substitutes correctly into A = P(1 − R)^n: A = 42,000 × (1 − 0.15)^4 (accept 42,000 × 0.85^4)
Calculates the value after 4 years as $21,924 (correct to the nearest dollar)
Calculates the total depreciation as 42,000 − 21,924 = $20,076

questions.stem: Simplify (3a⁴)².
questions.explanation_en: Each term inside the brackets is squared: 3² = 9, and the indices multiply, 4×2 = 8, so the answer is 9a⁸. The two most common mistakes are writing the coefficient 3 as 6, or working out 4×2 as 6.
questions.source: Algebra Topic test + Solutions.pdf · Part A Q12 · 4-01_ Index Laws

questions.stem: Simplify 2m × 5m p × 3n.
questions.explanation_en: The coefficient is 2×5×3 = 30; m×m = m² because the indices are added, and p and n each appear once, giving 30m²np. Treating m×m as 2m gives 10m²np, and treating it as m³ gives the wrong index.
questions.source: Topic2 Algebra.pdf · 4-01 The index laws

questions.stem: Simplify (6x²y) ÷ (9xy³).
questions.explanation_en: The coefficient simplifies to 6/9 = 2/3; when dividing like bases you subtract the indices, so x²÷x = x and y÷y³ = 1/y². The answer is 2x/(3y²). Common mistakes include writing the index of y as 3, or forgetting to simplify the coefficient.
questions.source: 4-03_ Multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions.pdf

questions.stem: Expand and simplify (2x − 5)(3x + 7).
questions.explanation_en: Multiplying each term gives 6x² + 14x − 15x − 35 = 6x² − x − 35. The middle terms 14x − 15x = −x; if −15x is written as +15x, it results in errors like 6x² + 29x.
questions.source: 4-05_ Expanding Binomial Products.pdf · Algebra Topic test + Solutions.pdf Q24c

questions.stem: If (7g + 3)² = 49g² + hg + 9, what is the value of h?
questions.explanation_en: The middle term of the perfect square is 2×7g×3 = 42g, so h = 42. The most common mistake is calculating only 7×3 = 21, missing the 2 in the formula.
questions.source: Algebra Topic test + Solutions.pdf · Part A Q14(perfect squares)

questions.stem: Factorise each expression fully. (a) 12a²b − 21ab²  (b) x² + 7x + 10
questions.explanation_en: (a) Take the greatest common factor: the HCF of 12 and 21 is 3, and the common factor of the variables a and b is ab, resulting in 3ab; inside the brackets, 3ab×4a=12a²b and 3ab×(−7b)=−21ab². (b) Find two numbers with a sum of 7 and a product of 10, which are 5 and 2.
questions.source: 4-06 Factorising monic quadratics.pdf · 2025 BBHS 10 (5.2) T2 Q14

criteria.t: Factorises 12a²b − 21ab² as 3ab(4a − 7b), taking the highest common factor 3ab
Factorises x² + 7x + 10 as (x + 5)(x + 2)

questions.topic: Equations · Linear with unknowns both sides
questions.stem: Solve 9x + 10 = 7x − 6.
questions.explanation_en: Subtracting 7x and 10 from both sides gives 2x = −16, so x = −8. Common mistakes include forgetting to change the sign when moving the 10 (getting −2) or calculating −16 ÷ 2 as +8.
questions.source: Topic 2 Equations and Inequality.pdf · 6-01 Equations(Example 1c)

questions.stem: Solve the inequality −3(x − 2) ≥ 15.
questions.explanation_en: Expanding gives −3x + 6 ≥ 15, which simplifies to −3x ≥ 9; when dividing both sides by −3, the inequality sign must be reversed, resulting in x ≤ −3. This can be verified by substituting x = −4: −3(−6)=18 ≥ 15, which holds true.
questions.source: Topic 2 Equations and Inequality.pdf · 6-07 Solving inequalities (reverse the sign when dividing by a negative)

questions.answer: Multiply every term by 12: 4x − 3(x − 2) = 24, so 4x − 3x + 6 = 24 and x = 18.
questions.explanation_en: The least common multiple of 3 and 4 is 12. The negative sign before the second term must be multiplied into the brackets, becoming +6; writing it as −6 results in x = 30, which is a common mistake.
questions.source: Topic 2 Equations and Inequality.pdf · 6-02 Equations with algebraic fractions

criteria.t: Multiplies every term by the common denominator 12 and expands correctly: 4x − 3(x − 2) = 24, giving 4x − 3x + 6 = 24
Solves the resulting equation to x = 18

questions.stem: Solve the simultaneous equations 5x + 2y = 19 and 3x − 2y = 5.
questions.explanation_en: Adding the two equations eliminates y: 8x = 24, x = 3; substituting back into the first equation gives 2y = 19 − 15 = 4, y = 2. The distractor (4, −0.5) only satisfies the first equation and can be eliminated by substituting into the second.
questions.source: Topic 2 Simultaneous Equations.pdf · 9-02 The elimination method

questions.stem: At the school canteen, 3 sandwiches and 2 drinks cost $19.50, while 2 sandwiches and 3 drinks cost $18.00. Find the cost of one sandwich and one drink.
questions.answer: Solve 3s + 2d = 19.50 and 2s + 3d = 18.00 simultaneously: 5s = 22.50, so s = $4.50 and d = $3.00.
questions.explanation_en: List the two equations and then eliminate one variable (multiplying the first equation by 3 and the second by 2 gives 5s = 22.50). Substituting back to check gives 3×4.50+2×3 = $19.50, which is correct.
questions.source: Topic 2 Simultaneous Equations.pdf · 9-04 Simultaneous equations problems

criteria.t: Sets up the two equations 3s + 2d = 19.50 and 2s + 3d = 18.00
Eliminates one variable and finds s = $4.50 (e.g. 5s = 22.50)
Finds d = $3.00 and states both prices

questions.stem: Find the distance between the points (2, −1) and (5, 3).
questions.explanation_en: d = √[(5−2)² + (3−(−1))²] = √(9+16) = √25 = 5. Forgetting to take the square root results in 25, and adding the differences directly gives 7.
questions.source: Topic 1 Coordinate Geometry.pdf · 2-01 Length, midpoint and gradient of an interval

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the line passing through (2, 5) and (6, −3).
questions.explanation_en: The gradient is m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) = (−3−5)/(6−2) = −8/4 = −2, not −1/2 or 2.
questions.source: Topic 1 Coordinate Geometry.pdf · 2-01 Length, midpoint and gradient of an interval

questions.topic: Coordinate geometry · Equation of a line
questions.stem: Which equation describes the line with gradient 3 that passes through the point (2, −1)?
questions.explanation_en: Substituting into y = mx + b gives −1 = 3(2) + b, so b = −7, hence y = 3x − 7, not y = 3x − 1.
questions.source: Topic 1 Coordinate Geometry.pdf · 2-06 Finding the equation of a line

questions.stem: Find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to y = 2x + 5 and passes through the point (4, 1). Give your answer in the form y = mx + b.
questions.answer: The perpendicular gradient is −1/2, so y − 1 = −1/2 (x − 4), which gives y = −1/2 x + 3.
questions.explanation_en: For perpendicular lines the product of the gradients is −1, so the gradient is −1/2; then substitute (4, 1) to find the y-intercept, which is 3.
questions.source: Topic 1 Coordinate Geometry.pdf · 2-07 Equations of parallel and perpendicular lines

criteria.t: States that the perpendicular gradient is −1/2 (the negative reciprocal of 2, not −2)
Substitutes (4, 1) and this gradient into y = mx + b (or point–gradient form) to find the intercept b = 3
Gives the final equation y = −1/2 x + 3

questions.stem: y varies directly as x. If y = 12 when x = 5, find x when y = 30.
questions.explanation_en: For direct proportion, write y = kx, find k = 12/5 = 2.4, then when y = 30, x = 30 ÷ 2.4 = 12.5, not 72.
questions.source: Topic 1 Graphs.pdf · 7-01 Direct proportion

questions.stem: y is inversely proportional to x. When x = 5, y = 8. Find y when x = 20.
questions.explanation_en: For inverse proportion, write y = k/x, find k = 40 from 5×8, then when x = 20, y = 40/20 = 2, not 32.
questions.source: Topic 1 Graphs.pdf · 7-02 Inverse proportion

questions.stem: A circle has equation x² + y² = 49. State its centre and radius, and determine whether the point (5, 5) lies on the circle.
questions.answer: Centre (0, 0) and radius 7. The point (5, 5) does not lie on the circle, because 5² + 5² = 50, not 49.
questions.explanation_en: The circle with equation x² + y² = r² has its centre at the origin and radius r = √49 = 7, so check if points are on the circle by substituting their coordinates.
questions.source: Topic 1 Graphs.pdf · 7-06 The circle

criteria.t: States the centre (0, 0) and the radius 7
Determines that (5, 5) is not on the circle because 5² + 5² = 50, not 49

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has two shorter sides of 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse.
questions.explanation_en: The hypotenuse is √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 cm, not 21 cm or 225 cm.
questions.source: Topic 3 Trigonometry.pdf · 8-01 Pythagoras' theorem

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle an angle is 35° and the side adjacent to it is 12 m. Find the length of the opposite side, correct to two decimal places.
questions.explanation_en: tan 35° = opposite side/adjacent side, so the opposite side is 12 × tan 35° ≈ 8.40 m, not 6.88 m or 17.14 m.
questions.source: Topic 3 Trigonometry.pdf · 8-03 Finding an unknown side

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, sin θ = 7/12. Find θ, correct to one decimal place.
questions.source: Topic 3 Trigonometry.pdf · 8-04 Finding an unknown angle

questions.stem: From a point on level ground 45 m from the base of a vertical tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is 62°. Find the height of the tower, correct to one decimal place.
questions.explanation_en: The angle of elevation uses tan, with 45 m as the adjacent side to 62°, so use tan, not sin, which would give 39.7 m.
questions.source: Topic 3 Trigonometry.pdf · 8-05 Angles of elevation and depression

criteria.t: Sets up tan 62° = h / 45 (chooses tan, treating 45 m as the side adjacent to the angle)
Calculates h = 45 × tan 62° ≈ 84.6 m

questions.stem: A plane flies 15 km due north and then 20 km due east. Find (a) its distance from the starting point and (b) its bearing from the starting point, correct to the nearest degree.
questions.answer: Distance = √(15² + 20²) = 25 km. Bearing = tan⁻¹(20/15) ≈ 53°, measured clockwise from north, so the bearing is 053°.
questions.explanation_en: The bearing is measured clockwise from north: the displacement is «15 north, 20 east», so the angle is 53° east of north, not 037°.
questions.source: Topic 3 Trigonometry.pdf · 8-06 Bearings / 8-07 Problems involving bearings

criteria.t: Calculates the distance from the start as √(15² + 20²) = 25 km
Finds the angle tan⁻¹(20/15) ≈ 53° east of north
States the bearing as 053° (measured clockwise from north, written as a three-figure bearing)

questions.stem: A cylinder has a diameter of 14 cm and a height of 20 cm. Find its volume, correct to one decimal place.
questions.explanation_en: First, find the radius r = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm, then V = πr²h = π × 49 × 20 = 980π ≈ 3078.8 cm³, not 12315.0 cm³.
questions.source: Topic3 Surface area and Volume.pdf · 3-05 Volumes of prisms and cylinders(V = πr²h)

questions.stem: A shape is made by attaching a semicircle of radius 4 cm to one side of a rectangle measuring 12 cm by 8 cm. Find the total area, correct to one decimal place.
questions.explanation_en: The rectangle is 12 × 8 = 96 cm², the semicircle is ½ × π × 4² = 8π ≈ 25.13 cm², for a total of ≈ 121.1 cm². Forgetting to halve it results in 146.3, and only calculating a quarter circle results in 108.6.
questions.source: Topic3 Surface area and Volume.pdf · 3-01 Areas of composite shapes

questions.topic: Surface area · Cylinder and paint cost
questions.stem: A cylindrical water tank has a radius of 5 m and a height of 10 m. Its entire surface, including the top and the bottom, is to be painted. (a) Find the total surface area, correct to the nearest square metre. (b) If paint costs $12 per square metre, find the total cost.
questions.explanation_en: Two circular faces and one side face total 150π. Calculating only the side face (100π ≈ 314 m²) misses the top and bottom; if the middle value is not rounded and 471.24 × 12 is used to get $5,654.88, it is also correct.
questions.source: 2025 BBHS 10 (5.2) T2 - soln.pdf · Q19 · Topic3 Surface area and Volume.pdf

criteria.t: Uses the correct total surface area formula 2πr² + 2πrh (both circular ends plus the curved surface)
Calculates the surface area as 150π ≈ 471 m² (accept 471.24 m²)
Calculates the cost as 471 × 12 ≈ $5,652 (accept $5,654.88 if the unrounded area is used)

questions.stem: A data distribution has a long tail extending towards the higher scores. How is this distribution described?
questions.explanation_en: A positively skewed distribution has its tail pointing to the high score side, while a negatively skewed distribution has its tail pointing to the low score side. The easiest way to remember this is by the phrase 'the tail swings to the side it's biased to'.
questions.source: Topic 1 Investigating Data.pdf · 5-01 The shape of a frequency distribution

questions.stem: Find the interquartile range of the data set 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22.
questions.explanation_en: With n = 10, the median is (12+15)/2 = 13.5; the lower quartile Q1 is 7 and the upper quartile Q3 is 18, so the IQR is 18 − 7 = 11. Choosing 13.5 is incorrect because it's the median, not the IQR.
questions.source: Topic 1 Investigating Data.pdf · 5-02 Quartiles and interquartile range

questions.stem: The ages of 13 participants in a sports event are: 12, 14, 15, 16, 17, 17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 25, 27, 30. (a) Write the five-number summary. (b) Calculate the interquartile range. (c) State, with a reason, whether the distribution is symmetrical or skewed.
questions.answer: (a) Lowest 12, Q1 = 15.5, median = 18, Q3 = 23.5, highest 30. (b) IQR = 23.5 − 15.5 = 8. (c) Positively skewed, because the upper whisker (23.5 to 30) is longer than the lower whisker (12 to 15.5).
questions.explanation_en: For 13 numbers, the median is the 7th number, and Q1 and Q3 are the medians of the lower and upper 6 numbers respectively. The upper whisker being 6.5 and the lower whisker being 3.5 indicates a longer tail on the high score side, so it's positively skewed.
questions.source: Topic 1 Investigating Data.pdf · 5-03 Boxplots · 2025 BBHS 10 (5.2) T2 - soln.pdf Q9

criteria.t: Writes the five-number summary 12, 15.5, 18, 23.5, 30 (lowest, Q1, median, Q3, highest)
Calculates the interquartile range as 23.5 − 15.5 = 8
States that the distribution is positively skewed
Justifies the skew: the upper whisker (23.5 to 30) is longer than the lower whisker (12 to 15.5)

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, 18 play soccer, 12 play basketball and 6 play both. How many students play neither sport?
questions.explanation_en: The number of people who can do at least one activity is 18 + 12 − 6 = 24, where the intersection of 6 people is counted twice and must be subtracted. So, the number of people who can do neither activity is 30 − 24 = 6. Forgetting to subtract the intersection results in 0.
questions.source: Topic 3 Probability.pdf · 10-02 Venn diagrams

questions.stem: Year 11 students were surveyed about part-time work. The results were: male with part-time work 43, male without part-time work 27, female with part-time work 35, female without part-time work 31. What is the probability that a randomly selected student works part-time, given that the student is male?
questions.explanation_en: The denominator of the conditional probability must be the total number of boys, which is 43 + 27 = 70, so it's 43/70. Using the total number of students (43/136) or the total number of part-time workers (43/78) as the denominator is incorrect because it doesn't account for the condition.
questions.source: Topic 3 Probability.pdf · 10-03 Two-way tables(Example 5)

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red and 5 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random one after the other without replacement. Find the probability that both marbles are red.
questions.explanation_en: For sampling without replacement, the sample space for the second draw is reduced by one ball, so it's 3/8 × 2/7. Writing it as 3/8 × 3/8 is incorrect because it assumes replacement.
questions.source: Topic 3 Probability.pdf · 10-05 Selecting with and without replacement

criteria.t: Multiplies the probabilities for the two draws without replacement: 3/8 × 2/7
Simplifies to 6/56 = 3/28

questions.stem: Priya's records for the financial year show: wages $62,400, bank interest $310, a $200 bonus, private school fees $4,800, work-related tool expenses $680, a donation to charity $150, a speeding fine $420 and her tax agent's fee $120. Using Taxable income = gross income − allowable deductions, calculate her taxable income.
questions.explanation_en: The total income is $62,400 + $310 + $200 = $62,910; only expenses and donations related to earning income are deductible: $680 for tools + $150 for donations + $120 for tax agent fees = $950, so the taxable income is $61,960. Private school fees and fines are not allowable deductions, and deducting them results in an incorrect answer of $56,740.
questions.source: 1-02_ Income tax.pdf(Taxable income = gross income − allowable deductions)· 2022 Year 10 5.2 Term 1 Revision Booklet.pdf · Exercise 1J

questions.stem: Australian resident tax rates — $0–$18,200: Nil; $18,201–$37,000: 19c for each $1 over $18,200; $37,001–$80,000: $3,572 plus 32.5c for each $1 over $37,000; $80,001–$180,000: $17,547 plus 37c for each $1 over $80,000; $180,001 and over: $54,547 plus 45c for each $1 over $180,000. Calculate the income tax payable on a taxable income of $30,000.
questions.explanation_en: The $30,000 falls in the 19c bracket: 0.19 × (30,000 − 18,200) = 0.19 × 11,800 = $2,242. The tax-free threshold of $18,200 must be subtracted first; directly using 0.19 × 30,000 results in $5,700, and $11,800 is the result of subtracting the threshold but not multiplying by the tax rate.
questions.source: 2022 Year 10 5.2 Term 1 Revision Booklet.pdf · Exercise 1J Q5a (official answer $2,242) · 1-02_ Income tax.pdf

questions.stem: Australian resident tax rates — $0–$18,200: Nil; $18,201–$37,000: 19c for each $1 over $18,200; $37,001–$80,000: $3,572 plus 32.5c for each $1 over $37,000; $80,001–$180,000: $17,547 plus 37c for each $1 over $80,000; $180,001 and over: $54,547 plus 45c for each $1 over $180,000. Calculate the income tax payable on a taxable income of $150,000.
questions.explanation_en: The $150,000 is in the 37c bracket: $17,547 + 0.37 × (150,000 − 80,000) = $17,547 + $25,900 = $43,447. Two common errors are omitting the base amount (0.37 × 150,000 = $55,500) and using the wrong base (using the top of the previous bracket to get $80,447); $40,297 is the result of using the wrong tax rate of 32.5c.
questions.source: 2022 Year 10 5.2 Term 1 Revision Booklet.pdf · Exercise 1J Q5c (official answer $43,447)

questions.stem: Australian resident tax rates — $0–$18,200: Nil; $18,201–$37,000: 19c for each $1 over $18,200; $37,001–$80,000: $3,572 plus 32.5c for each $1 over $37,000; $80,001–$180,000: $17,547 plus 37c for each $1 over $80,000; $180,001 and over: $54,547 plus 45c for each $1 over $180,000. Ann's taxable income is $80,000 and Ben's is $80,001. Ignoring the Medicare levy, calculate the tax each person pays and state how much more tax Ben pays than Ann.
questions.explanation_en: The tax brackets are continuous: the top of the 32.5c bracket ($17,547) is exactly the base amount of the 37c bracket, so Ben pays 37c on the extra $1, a difference of only 37 cents.
questions.source: 2022 Year 10 5.2 Term 1 Revision Booklet.pdf · Exercise 1J Q4 (official answer: 37 cents)

criteria.t: Calculates Ben's tax as $17,547 + 0.37 × 1 = $17,547.37 (only the $1 above $80,000 is taxed at 37c)
States that Ben pays 37 cents more than Ann

questions.stem: Australian resident tax rates — $0–$18,200: Nil; $18,201–$37,000: 19c for each $1 over $18,200; $37,001–$80,000: $3,572 plus 32.5c for each $1 over $37,000; $80,001–$180,000: $17,547 plus 37c for each $1 over $80,000; $180,001 and over: $54,547 plus 45c for each $1 over $180,000. Kim's gross pay for the year is $54,300. She has no allowable deductions, so her taxable income is also $54,300. Calculate (a) her income tax payable and (b) her net pay, given that she also pays $960 in other deductions (union fees and health fund contributions).
questions.explanation_en: The formula is net pay = gross pay − tax − other deductions, so both tax and other deductions must be subtracted. Subtracting only tax gives $45,105.50, which is the main error in this question.
questions.source: 1-02_ Income tax.pdf(Net pay = gross pay − tax − other deduction; Example 3)

criteria.t: Subtracts both the tax and the other deductions: 54,300 − 9,194.50 − 960
Gives the net pay as $44,145.50

questions.stem: Two netball teams each score a mean of 24 goals per game over a season. Team A's scores have a standard deviation of 2.1 goals and Team B's have a standard deviation of 6.4 goals. What does this tell you?
options: Team B scored more goals in total than Team A.
Both teams had exactly the same range of scores.
Team A's standard deviation must be wrong, because both teams have the same mean.
Team A's scores were more consistent from game to game than Team B's.
questions.explanation_en: The standard deviation measures the spread of the data around the mean: when two means are equal, a larger standard deviation means more variation in the scores, so Team A is the more consistent team. Standard deviation is unrelated to the total score and is not the same as the range, so the first two options cannot be concluded.
questions.source: New Century 10 Standard-Core Textbook.pdf · 5.03 Standard deviation · 2025 BBHS 10 (5.2) T2 Ana (IntDep+Alg+Data+Pav).pdf Q7(e)

questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of the data set 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, correct to one decimal place. Use σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n).
questions.explanation_en: The mean x̄ = 40 ÷ 8 = 5, the sum of squared deviations = 9+1+1+1+0+0+4+16 = 32, and σ = √(32 ÷ 8) = √4 = 2.0; choosing 4.0 forgets to take the square root (that's variance), and 2.1 is the sample standard deviation divided by n−1.
questions.source: New Century 10 Standard-Core Textbook.pdf · 5.03 Standard deviation(σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n))

questions.stem: A team scored the following number of goals in its 10 matches: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5, 6. (a) Find the mean. (b) Find the standard deviation, correct to two decimal places, using σ = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n).
questions.explanation_en: First, find the mean 2.5, then calculate the squared deviations individually: 6.25+2.25+2.25+0.25+0.25+0.25+0.25+0.25+6.25+12.25 = 30.5, and after dividing by n=10 and taking the square root, the result is 1.75; this question uses the population standard deviation (divided by n), and if divided by n−1=9, the result would be 1.84, which is the sample standard deviation.
questions.source: 2025 BBHS 10 (5.2) T2 Ana (IntDep+Alg+Data+Pav).pdf · Q7(e) · New Century 10 Standard-Core Textbook.pdf · 5.03

criteria.t: Finds the mean as 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5 goals
Calculates the sum of squared deviations, Σ(x − 2.5)² = 30.5
Calculates σ = √(30.5 ÷ 10) ≈ 1.75 goals (correct to two decimal places)

questions.stem: In a network diagram, the number of edges meeting at a vertex is called its:
questions.explanation_en: The number of edges connected to a vertex is called the degree, and the number of vertices with odd degrees determines whether it can be drawn in one stroke: all even → can return to the starting point; exactly two odd → can be drawn in one stroke but with a different ending point.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · Mathematics Core/Standard(Networks: terminology)

questions.stem: A connected network has vertices with degrees 2, 2, 4, 2, 2. Which statement is true?
options: It has an Eulerian circuit because every vertex has even degree
It has exactly one odd vertex
It cannot be drawn without lifting the pen
questions.explanation_en: If every vertex has an even degree, the graph has an Eulerian circuit: start anywhere, traverse each edge once and return to the starting point. If any vertex has an odd degree, that is not possible.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · Mathematics Standard(Eulerian trails and circuits)

questions.stem: A network has exactly two vertices of odd degree. What can be concluded?
options: An Eulerian trail exists, starting and finishing at the two odd-degree vertices
Every vertex must be visited twice
questions.explanation_en: Having exactly two odd-degree vertices → there is an Eulerian path (can be drawn in one stroke), which must start from one odd vertex and end at the other; to return to the starting point (a circuit), all vertices must have even degrees.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · Mathematics Standard(Eulerian trials and circuits)

questions.stem: A town must connect four buildings with cable at minimum total length. The possible connections and lengths (km) are AB 2, AC 5, BC 3, BD 4, CD 1. What is the minimum total length?
questions.explanation_en: The minimum spanning tree = select 3 edges to connect the whole without forming a cycle; sort by length: CD 1, AB 2, BC 3 → the three edges connect A-B-C-D without a cycle, with a total length of 1+2+3=6; adding any other edge would form a cycle.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · Mathematics Core/Standard(Shortest path and minimum spanning trees)

questions.stem: Using the network in which AB = 2, BC = 3, AC = 5, BD = 4 and CD = 1 (all in km), what is the shortest distance from A to D?
questions.explanation_en: All routes go through C or B: A→B→D=6, A→B→C→D=6, A→C→D=6, and the shortest is 6 km, so the answer is 6 km.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · Mathematics Core/Standard(Shortest path)

questions.stem: A planar graph is one that:
options: Can be drawn on a plane without any edges crossing
Has all vertices of equal degree
Contains no more than four vertices
questions.explanation_en: A planar graph refers to a graph that can be drawn on a plane without any edges intersecting; whether it looks intersecting or not is irrelevant, what matters is whether it can be redrawn without intersecting.
questions.source: Yearly Study Guide 2026 · Mathematics Core(Network terminology and planar graphs)
